opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it comes down to wanting every experiment to teach me something, no matter how it turns out.

A lot of research is set up as a one-sided bet. You have an idea, you think it'll work, and you run the experiment hoping to show it does. If it works, great, you have a paper. If it doesn't, you've usually learned very little. Maybe your idea was wrong, maybe your hyperparameters were off, maybe there was a bug. You can't tell, so the negative result ends up in a drawer.

A two-sided question is one where either answer is interesting. The lottery ticket work is a good example. The question was basically: can we find small subnetworks, at or near initialization, that train to full accuracy on their own? If the answer is yes, that's surprising and tells us something about why overparameterization helps and how pruning works. If the answer is no, that's also informative. It tells us those sparse networks really need the dense training process, and that the structure pruning finds only emerges later. Either way you've learned something real about how neural networks behave.

I think that framing also makes you a more honest scientist. When you're invested in one outcome, it's tempting to keep tweaking until you get the answer you wanted. When both outcomes are valuable, you're much more willing to let the data speak, and you design cleaner experiments because you actually care about distinguishing the two possibilities.

It also suits where deep learning is as a field. We still don't have a great understanding of why a lot of this works. In that setting, I think carefully posed questions that map out what's true are often worth more than another method that adds a point of accuracy on a benchmark. Two-sided questions push you toward understanding rather than just engineering, and I think we need much more of that.

r001.rationale: The response says either outcome of a two-sided question is informative: “Either way you've learned something real.”

r002.rationale: It discusses whether subnetworks at initialization can train to full accuracy, but does not ask when the eventual optimum becomes determined during training.

r003.rationale: It does not connect two-sided questions to reducing PhD students’ anxiety.

r004.rationale: It advocates two-sided questions but does not suggest that most research questions can be reformulated that way.

r005.rationale: The response mentions hyperparameters or bugs as possible explanations for failed one-sided experiments, but does not say that failing to find lottery tickets could reflect an inadequate search method rather than their nonexistence.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it comes down to a lesson I learned the hard way during my PhD. When I was working on the lottery ticket hypothesis, I spent a lot of time chasing experiments where I'd basically already decided what the answer should be. I wanted sparse subnetworks to train well in isolation, so I'd set up an experiment, and if it worked, great, I'd write it up. If it didn't, I'd think, "well, something must be wrong with my setup," and I'd go tweak things until it did. That's a terrible way to do science, and I think a lot of us in deep learning fall into it because the field moves so fast and there's so much pressure to have a positive result.

So now, before I run an experiment, I try to force myself to ask: what do I learn if the answer comes back the other way? If I can't articulate why the negative result would be interesting, that's a red flag. It usually means I'm not actually asking a question, I'm just trying to confirm a belief. And a confirmation isn't very informative. If I was already ninety percent sure something would work, and it works, I've updated by ten percent. Big deal.

The two-sided framing also keeps me honest about what the paper is going to say. With the lottery ticket work, the really interesting thing wasn't just "here are these winning tickets." It was that at larger scale, the simple version of the procedure stopped working, and we had to understand why. That failure told us something about how early in training the network's trajectory gets determined, and that turned into a whole line of work on stability and the early phase of training. If I'd treated the failure as an embarrassment to be hidden, we would have missed the most useful finding.

And frankly, there's a practical side too. Deep learning is an empirical science right now, whether we like it or not. We don't have the theory to tell us in advance what should happen. So the only tool we really have is careful experiments, and careful experiments are ones where both outcomes mean something. Otherwise you're just running a very expensive demo.

r001.rationale: The response says careful experiments are ones where “both outcomes mean something” and asks what can be learned if the result goes the other way.

r002.rationale: It says the network’s trajectory is determined early in training, but does not pose the specific question of when the eventual optimum becomes determined.

r003.rationale: The response mentions research pressure, but does not identify two-sided questions as a way to reduce PhD students’ anxiety about whether their research will work.

r004.rationale: It recommends considering what a contrary result would teach, but does not say that most research questions can be reformulated as two-sided questions.

r005.rationale: It describes the lottery ticket procedure stopping working at larger scale, but does not explain that failing to find tickets could mean either that none exist or that the method is inadequate.

astra-6.text:
I like questions where either answer would teach us something. Research is uncertain, and if the only interesting outcome is that your hypothesis is right, you can spend a lot of time getting a result you don’t know what to do with. There’s also a temptation to keep pushing until you get the answer you wanted.

With a two-sided question, you can say, “If this works, that opens up an opportunity. If it doesn’t, that tells us something important about the limits of our approach.” You still need a careful experiment—a failed experiment doesn’t automatically establish that something is impossible—but you’re setting yourself up to learn rather than just to confirm a belief. That makes a question much more appealing to me.

r001.rationale: It says either answer would teach something and explains that both success and failure can provide useful knowledge.

r002.rationale: It does not ask when the eventual optimum becomes determined during neural network training.

r003.rationale: It does not mention PhD students or reducing their anxiety about research outcomes.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest that most research questions can be reformulated as two-sided questions.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss lottery tickets or distinguish their nonexistence from an inadequate search method.

sol-6.1.text: I like questions where either answer would be interesting. If you ask, “Can we do this?” and the only exciting outcome is yes, then you can spend a lot of time on something and come away with very little to say. But if the answer is no, and that tells us something meaningful about how neural networks work, then you’ve learned something either way. It forces you to think about what you’re actually trying to understand, rather than just the result you’re hoping to get.
